Their positions connected money to force. The ship was a workplace, a prison, a transport vessel, and a legal object at once. Those functions could not be reduced to a single arithmetic of profit.

Rejecting a purely economic explanation does not turn the Zong into an eruption of private cruelty detached from Atlantic commerce. The claim arose because the killings could be presented as the destruction of insurable property. The owners’ effort to recover money was not an afterthought. It was the route by which the event entered the London courts and later contributed, according to the legal commentary, to a statutory prohibition.

The commercial form helped conceal the killing and helped expose it. The same system that rendered enslaved people transferable and insurable generated records through which the violence could later be challenged. The policy treated them as property; the dispute made that treatment visible. The law’s attention was narrow, but its narrowness became evidence. A technical controversy about whether an insured loss had occurred opened a public view onto the practice of killing captives at sea.

The legislative response confirms the limits of the reform. Parliament prohibited insurance claims for slaves thrown overboard “on any account whatsoever”, yet preserved cover for “the perils of the seas, piracy, insurrection, capture, barratry, and destruction by fire.” Commercial calculation formed part of the dispute, but the law did more than adjust the price of jettisoning. It removed insurance support for that act while leaving the categories of ownership and maritime risk that made the Zong voyage profitable and its dead claimable.

Racial ideology was not merely a justification added after the economic system had begun. It helped determine whose death could be argued as a loss and whose safety could be weighed against the safety of others. A person represented as property could be insured. A person confined within that classification could be killed under a claim of necessity, while the legal process heard the owners’ account rather than the captives’ testimony. These arrangements supported one another.

Profit supplied an incentive. Ownership supplied a legal status. Race supplied a hierarchy of human value. Maritime command supplied the means. Insurance supplied a language of loss. Litigation supplied a public record. Each element changed what the others could do. The killing became both an act of physical violence and an event processed by commercial administration.

The record does not supply a full account of plantation life or of the communities from which the captives came. The Zong had left the coast of Guinea and was bound for Jamaica, but the legal materials do not identify the Africans by name, region, language, age beyond the categories of women, children, and males, or family relationship. Their prior lives remain outside the insurance claim. The court could determine an amount without recovering a biography.

On the ship, the account records fragments rather than a continuous scene. Fifty-four women and children were thrown through cabin windows on 29 November. Forty-two males were killed on 1 December. Thirty-six more followed. Ten people jumped into the sea, one person climbed back aboard, and one captive’s request was ignored. These actions are preserved because they bear on the historical account of the massacre, yet the source gives no sustained testimony from those who performed or endured them. The legal and commercial form that made the case produced the missing voices.

Plantation life appears only as the destination that gave the voyage its purpose. Jamaica is the intended port, then the place where the Zong arrived with 420 imperial gallons of water on 22 December. The island’s plantations, markets, punishments, and enslaved communities do not enter the proceedings. Nor can the Zong record establish how resistance operated elsewhere in the Atlantic. It shows one route by which violence became administratively legible, not the experience of every Atlantic society.

The absences have a history. The people most vulnerable to violence were often least able to enter the records later inherited by historians. Owners, captains, insurers, lawyers, judges, and legislators left documents because their work required contracts, affidavits, judgments, and statutes. The enslaved were recorded as numbers, cargo, labourers, offenders, or losses. Their resistance sometimes appears in a sentence, as with the captive who asked that food and drink be withheld rather than more people thrown overboard. The form of the record makes such a sentence precious and insufficient at once.

By the time the Zong dispute reached the Guildhall, the killings had passed through several classifications. At sea they were presented as a response to navigational error and water shortage. In the insurance claim they were a possible loss of property. In the courtroom they became evidence about a maritime contract. In the later legislative response they became the occasion for prohibiting a specific insurance claim. For the Africans who died, none of those classifications displaced the physical fact of being forced into the water.

The legal record obscures their lives, but it also reveals the architecture that obscured them. A ship could carry people as cargo; a plantation economy could demand their labour; a racial order could define them as property; an insurance policy could assign a monetary value; and a courtroom could decide whether their destruction qualified for compensation. The chain operated through named places, dates, documents, offices, and decisions.

The Zong reveals how commercial institutions gave killing a form in which it could be claimed, disputed, measured, and eventually restricted. The dead entered the public record through a lawsuit that treated them as property. That fact is neither the whole history of the massacre nor a neutral description of it. It is the form through which a racialised order made human destruction administratively visible.

chapters.title: Gunpowder, Bureaucracy, and Mass Mobilization
chapters.markdown:
In the beginning of the 1680s, Charles XI faced an army whose condition had been judged bad during the Scanian War of 1674–1679. The account of the allotment system places his decision in 1682: he reorganised the army and introduced a system that would remain in effect for more than two centuries. Hans Högman dates the parliamentary act more precisely to October 27 of that year and gives it the name by which it became known, Indelningsverket, or the Allotment System. The date belongs to a decision by the Crown and Parliament. Its consequences were distributed among counties, parishes, freeholders, soldiers, and the farms that supported them.

The Military Act attached obligations to places rather than beginning with an abstract population. Contracts were drawn up between the Crown and the freeholders of each province. A county or province undertook to raise and supply a regiment in wartime and peacetime; the account summarised by Wikipedia gives the possible size as 1,000 or 1,200 men, while Högman describes each infantry regiment as numbering 1,200. The discrepancy is small beside the administrative fact: a military unit was connected to a specified territory. The contracts provided for soldiers, equipment, crofts, farmland, and regiments through arrangements intended to persist.

Högman calls participation mandatory for the freeholders. His description is emphatic about the burden. “To maintain a soldier for the regiment was costly and an extra burden to the farmers,” he writes in his account of the 1682 system. The Crown did not merely request a contribution from a rural population, and the farmer did not merely pay a tax whose military destination vanished from sight. The rote became responsible for a particular kind of maintenance: a soldier, his equipment, a croft, and land attached to that croft. A fiscal demand took a social and material form.

The system preserved a distinction between the person who served and the people who supported him. The farms in a district joined to equip one soldier, while the rest of the men in those farms avoided conscription, according to the Wikipedia account. Högman describes the district, or rote, as generally consisting of two to four farmers, and says that the costs were shared among them. Wikipedia commonly describes four farms joining together, while also noting exceptions. The sources disagree over the usual size of the contributing group, but they agree about the principle: several freeholders could be bound together so that one soldier’s provision would not fall upon a single household. That division made the obligation practicable without making it voluntary. A province could be made answerable for a regiment; a parish could be divided into rotar; a rote could be made answerable for one soldier. Each level narrowed a large military demand into a responsibility that could be assigned, inspected, and sustained. The chain gave the Crown a way to reach the countryside without requiring every farmer to become a soldier, while giving the countryside a way to distribute the cost among recognisable units.

The soldier’s residence was part of this arrangement. The rote supplied a soldattorp, or soldier croft, with farmland, as well as equipment. Högman explains that the croft was a small homestead where the soldier lived when he was not serving in the regiment. The sources describe the soldier as a volunteer who could make a military career. His home, land, uniform, and place in the regiment were linked by the allotment agreement, although the passages describing the system do not identify the individuals who filled those places.

The cavalry required a different local contribution. Each rusthåll provided a horse and horseman. In earlier years the rider was often the farmer himself; later, according to the Wikipedia account, the horseman became a volunteer supplied with a croft and paid by the farmer. In return, the farmer received a substantial tax reduction and exemption from army service. The rationale given in the same account was practical: a fallen horseman was easier to replace than the master of an estate. A rusthåll usually consisted of one estate, perhaps with a supporting farmer, though exceptional cases could support as many as seven horsemen.

The cavalry example shows that the Crown did not extract identical service from every rural producer. One estate might supply a horseman, receive tax relief, and avoid the farmer’s own service; several farms might support an infantry soldier; another man might occupy the croft and serve as the trained member of the regiment. Military duties, tax reductions, and exemptions were distributed through different arrangements. The system’s usefulness depended on placing different burdens on different holders of land and property.

Sweden and Finland were both included in the standing army described by Högman. The arrangement also rested on earlier organisational work. Under Gustav II Adolf, the Swedish armed forces had been modernised tactically and organisationally; Högman dates the reorganisation of units into modern regiments to 1623 and says that at least one regiment was stationed in each province. The Constitution Act of 1634 adopted that organisation, specifying twenty infantry regiments, thirteen in real Sweden and seven in Finland, alongside eight cavalry regiments, five in real Sweden and three in Finland. The 1682 act attached a more durable pattern of obligation to a territorial structure already associated with provincial regiments, building on existing military administration.

The sequence from 1623 to 1682 is not a smooth story of inevitable improvement. Högman presents the earlier regimental structure, while the later account identifies the Scanian War as one reason for reorganising an army judged to be in poor condition. The system’s persistence for more than 200 years indicates durability, not universal efficiency or uniform acceptance. A contract could define a duty without revealing how a farmer regarded it, how a soldier entered the service, or how a province absorbed the cost. The statute names the parties to an obligation. It does not supply their voices.

The act connected provincial contracts, parish districts, crofts, and equipment. It reached farms without dissolving them into a wholly state-owned apparatus. The army remained dependent on rural households, yet those households were made part of a continuing military system. Sweden’s military capacity was distributed across a countryside whose land, labour, animals, exemptions, and payments had been connected to the army by rule.

The important actor in this portrait is consequently not Charles XI in isolation, though his decision stands at its beginning. It is the relation established between Charles XI, the Parliament of 1682, the provinces, and the freeholders. The act converted a need for soldiers into obligations that could persist beyond the moment that produced them. The contracts specified duties for provinces and freeholders, and the farms provided the soldiers, equipment, crofts, and farmland described in the accounts.

The arrangement becomes clearer when followed from the farm outward. Contracts were drawn up with the Crown and the farmers or freeholders in each province. The contract stated that the province would raise and supply a regiment, described as 1,000 or 1,200 men in the Wikipedia account, or as 1,200 in Högman’s description. The province’s obligation was both wartime and peacetime. Within the province, parishes were divided into allotments called rotar. Two to four farmers generally shared one rote in Högman’s account, while the Wikipedia description gives four farms as the usual pattern and notes exceptions.

The rote had one defined task: provide and maintain an infantry soldier. Maintenance included the soldier’s equipment, a uniform among the items specified by Högman, and a soldattorp with farmland. The rote maintained the croft for the soldier to live in when he was not serving in the regiment. The sources describe the soldier as a volunteer, even though the freeholders’ participation was mandatory, and say that he could make a military career. One person served, while several farms shared the cost of maintaining him.

The cavalry route began from the rusthåll rather than the infantry rote. A rusthåll usually consisted of one estate and perhaps another supporting farmer. It provided a horse and horseman, later furnishing the rider with a croft and pay while receiving tax reduction. In this case the farm’s contribution was not divided in precisely the same way as the infantry obligation. The army needed a mounted man, while the rural arrangement gave the estate holder an exemption from army service and made replacement easier if the horseman fell.

Training and equipment changed the speed of mobilisation. The Wikipedia account contrasts the Swedish system with the time required to enlist, equip, train, and organise mercenaries, which could take weeks or months. Croft soldiers, by contrast, gathered at the company meeting place in a couple of days and then at the regimental meeting place in around a week. They were already trained and equipped, knew their place in the formation, and had prepared routes to borders or harbours. Supplies had been gathered at important places. These details describe the steps by which the order to mobilise became the assembly of a regiment.

The sequence began with land and continued to the soldier’s arrival at the company meeting place. A province’s farms supported a rote; the rote maintained a croft; the croft housed a soldier; the soldier possessed equipment; the soldier knew his position; the company had a place of assembly; the regiment had a larger place of assembly; routes and supplies had already been prepared. The sources describe these arrangements as the basis for quick gathering. They do not establish a broader order in which agricultural or residential readiness preceded operational readiness.

The earlier provincial organisation helped make this chain legible. Högman’s account of the 1623 regiments and the 1634 Constitution Act supplies the territorial background. The later allotment system connected a province already identified with a regiment to parishes and farms that could support the regiment’s men. The administrative map and the military map reinforced each other. Högman describes the result as a standing army, while the allotment accounts describe the crofts, equipment, meeting places, routes, and supplies through which soldiers were maintained and assembled.

The resulting capacity was considerable in relation to population, according to the Wikipedia account, which calls the Swedish army the largest in Europe in relation to population and describes its position in Northern Europe as unusual. Such comparisons cannot be measured here against a common standard for every army mentioned. The procedure itself is clear: croft soldiers could gather quickly because they were already trained and equipped, and because meeting places, routes, and supplies had been identified.

A farmer’s private motive does not explain that speed. The accounts attribute it to the arrangements of the allotment system: the croft soldiers gathered in a couple of days at the company meeting place and in around a week at the regimental meeting place. The Crown could call upon an army without beginning the work of finding every man, furnishing every uniform, and deciding every place in the line.

The Swedish case invites a familiar interpretation of early modern warfare. Gunpowder weapons were expensive; armies grew; rulers required more reliable revenue; bureaucratic states expanded to collect and direct resources. The general pattern has been called a “Military Revolution,” although the historical accounts describe the timing and character of that transformation as debated. Some historians see a profound change in warfare and state formation, while critics describe a longer evolutionary process and question whether technology alone explains the growth of armies. Sweden’s allotment system sits usefully inside that debate because it makes the social work of mobilisation visible.

The system rested on administrative organisation. The passages on Sweden describe contracts, farms, crofts, equipment, horses, tax reductions, meeting places, routes, and gathered supplies. Those details shift the question from what gunpowder did by itself to what a government and rural society had to organise before armed force could be used repeatedly.

Charles XI’s reform followed the bad condition of the army during the Scanian War, according to the Wikipedia account. That reason explains a pressure for reorganisation, but it does not establish every motive held by the Crown, the freeholders, or the soldiers. Nor does the existence of a standing system establish why Sweden would later choose a particular war. The capacity to assemble force and the decision to use force belong to different historical questions.

This separation is essential when military organisation is compared with the commercial violence described in the case of the Zong. In the Zong litigation, law organised a killing after the fact by giving it categories through which owners, insurers, and judges could dispute compensation. The Swedish allotment system organised military capacity through recurring duties. Both cases show people being made legible to an administrative order, although the orders differed. The Zong record concerns enslaved people treated as insured property and a legal dispute heard at the Guildhall on March 6, 1783. Sweden concerns freeholders, soldiers, parishes, and provinces joined to a Crown’s military demand. The comparison illuminates organisation without making the forms of harm interchangeable.

Nor should the Swedish system be read as evidence that bureaucracy produces aggression by itself. It produced a capacity for rapid assembly. That capacity could support defence, bargaining, deterrence, or war. The records here establish neither a particular Swedish campaign nor the intentions of each person within the system. A regiment that could gather in days possessed a different military reach from a force that had to be recruited and equipped from the beginning, but reach is not motive.

Technological explanations that place gunpowder at the centre of every change face the same limit. Artillery and firearms could increase the cost of fortification and the need for disciplined troops, as broader accounts of early modern warfare suggest. Sweden’s allotment procedure shows that their military use depended on arrangements that fed, housed, equipped, trained, and moved the people who used them. Administration was not a neutral instrument that merely carried out decisions made elsewhere. The Crown’s contracts altered rural duties. A farmer’s land was connected to a soldier’s uniform and croft. A tax reduction could exchange one kind of service for another. The arrangement distributed advantage and burden while creating a standing military body.

The public vocabulary of the system can obscure this material exchange. “Allotment” sounds like a division on paper, but the allotment was a farm obligation, a croft, a horse, a uniform, and a person expected to appear at a meeting place. “Recruitment” sounds like an individual choice, but the soldier’s possibility of service depended on the rote. “Mobilisation” sounds like a sudden command, but the quick assembly depended on work performed during peacetime. Each term points to an administrative action whose effects reached into households.

A state that could mobilise quickly might also govern more deeply, but the sources do not show how uniformly that depth was felt across Sweden and Finland. They name participating farmers as freeholders, describe mandatory participation, and identify the costs attached to maintaining soldiers. They do not give the voices of farmers discussing those costs, the choices of men who entered the crofts, or the local disputes through which obligations were settled. The institutional interpretation is strongest when it stays close to the procedure: the system enlarged the Crown’s military capacity by making rural society responsible for maintaining soldiers and their equipment.

The unresolved question lies on the other side of that responsibility. What did the allotment system feel like to the people whose farms sustained it?

The surviving description tells us that freeholders in Sweden and Finland were required to participate, that a rote of two to four farmers shared the maintenance of an infantry soldier, and that the burden included equipment, a croft, and farmland. It tells us that cavalry support could bring tax reduction, and that a soldier might live in the croft while pursuing a military career. These are substantial facts about obligation and provision. They do not disclose the arguments held in a parish, the pressure placed on a poorer farmer, or the meaning of the croft to the soldier who occupied it.

A provincial regiment could be a source of local identity, a demand imposed by the Crown, or both. The records describing the 1682 Military Act do not decide among those possibilities. Nor do they tell us how wives, children, tenants, servants, and neighbours experienced the absence or return of a soldier. The croft appears as a unit of military maintenance. Its domestic life remains outside the account. The system’s effectiveness depended on continuing work in counties, parishes, estates, and crofts: a route to a harbour, a gathered supply, a maintained horse, and an equipped soldier. How that work was negotiated, resisted, welcomed, or endured would alter the meaning of the system for the people who carried it.

The Swedish record makes the Crown’s reach visible. It leaves the civilian response partly beyond reach. That open space does not weaken the evidence for organised military capacity; it marks the distance between measuring what a state required and knowing how a society lived under the requirement.

chapters.title: Revolution and the Politics of the Crowd
chapters.markdown:
> “The Bastille loomed large in the French imagination as a mysterious, medieval, dark dungeon of a place where vast numbers of people who had displeased the King would disappear to lead a tortured existence. In fact, by the time of Louis XVI, living conditions inside the Bastille were not at all dire;”
>
> — National Archives exhibit text, *archives.gov*

On the afternoon of 14 July 1789, Monsieur de Corny, identified by Thomas Jefferson as a member of the States General, went towards the Bastille with five others. Their purpose was specific: in Jefferson’s account, they had been sent to ask the governor, Monsieur de Launay, for arms. A great collection of people had already gathered before the fortress, so the deputation did not create the assembly that received it. It entered a confrontation before a building whose military function and political reputation had become difficult to separate.

The deputies planted a flag of truce. A like flag appeared on the parapet. For a moment, the two signs established a language of controlled encounter, in which armed parties recognized a pause and allowed representatives to approach. Jefferson says that the deputation persuaded the people to fall back a little, then advanced to make its demand of the governor. The movement was small but consequential. The crowd withdrew; the deputies occupied the space between the people and the fortress.

Then, Jefferson wrote, a discharge from the Bastille killed four people nearest to the deputies. His account gives the gunfire a precise place in the sequence: the flag of truce had been raised, the people had withdrawn somewhat, and the deputies had advanced before the shots were fired. The passage does not preserve the full exchange between Corny and de Launay, nor does it record what either side believed the flags signified. It names the dead only as four people nearest to the deputies. Their names, positions, and purposes are absent, although their deaths become the immediate fact around which Jefferson orders the next movement.

The deputies retired. The crowd rushed against the Bastille.

Jefferson’s wording makes the transition abrupt. He says that the people were “almost in an instant” in possession of a fortification defended by 100 men, a place of “infinite strength” that had withstood several regular sieges and had never been taken. The contrast is between the fortress as a military object and the speed of its seizure. Yet the account does not tell how the crowd entered. Jefferson pauses over that gap: “How they got in, has as yet been impossible to discover.” Those who claimed to have been part of the assault offered so many different stories, he said, that their disagreements destroyed the credibility of all of them.

The uncertainty begins at the point where the action became most decisive. The Bastille was taken, but the passage cannot provide a reliable account of how the people crossed its defences. Jefferson’s sequence remains legible at several points: Corny and five others approached; a flag of truce was exchanged; four people were killed; the deputies withdrew; the crowd rushed; possession followed. The record establishes a change in political and physical control, while the conflicting stories prevent a precise reconstruction of the entry itself.

Once inside, the crowd took the arms. Jefferson says that it released the prisoners and those members of the garrison who had not been killed in the first moment of fury. The fortress therefore produced several outcomes at once. Its weapons changed hands. Its prisoners were freed. Some defenders survived through release, while others did not. The seizure was neither only an assault nor only a liberation. It rearranged possession, custody, and life within the same act.

The National Archives exhibit gives the prison population a sharply different scale from the one suggested by the Bastille’s reputation. On 14 July 1789, it says, the fortress held seven prisoners: two people who were mentally ill, four forgers, and one person incarcerated for incest. The exhibit describes the Bastille as a mysterious, medieval, dark dungeon in the French imagination, a place where vast numbers of people who had displeased the king were thought to disappear. It then places that image beside the seven actual prisoners and notes that conditions under Louis XVI were not at all dire by the standards implied by the legend: food was adequate, and prisoners could bring in many of their own possessions.

The difference between seven prisoners and the imagined multitude did not make the Bastille politically empty. A building can hold few captives and still signify a much wider power. The fortress stood for the king’s authority in a way that exceeded its current population, and its seizure made that authority physically vulnerable. Those who entered did not need to discover hundreds of prisoners for the building to serve as evidence of oppression in the revolutionary imagination. Its symbolic force was already attached to its walls, its governor, its arms, and its relationship to royal rule.

Jefferson’s account then turns from release to retaliation. The governor and lieutenant governor were carried to the Grève, which Jefferson identifies as the place of public execution. There, he says, the crowd cut off their heads and carried them through the city in triumph to the Palais Royal. The movement out of the Bastille gave the killing a public route. The violence did not remain within the fortress or end with the fall of its defences. The heads became objects in a procession, and the procession converted the deaths into a display before a wider Parisian audience.

The return procession placed the king’s carriage at its centre. Members of the States General walked on either side in two ranks, while the Marquis de la Fayette, commander in chief, rode at their head. Bourgeois guards stood before and behind. Around them, Jefferson estimated, were about 60,000 citizens “of all forms and colours”, many armed with muskets taken from the Bastille and the Invalids. Others carried pistols, swords, pikes, pruning hooks, and scythes. The weapons were not all military objects. Some belonged to ordinary work and had been brought into a public confrontation that now claimed the language of national power.

The streets, doors, and windows filled with people. Jefferson recorded cries of “vive la nation” and emphasized that not a single “vive le roy” was heard during the procession’s outward movement. At the Hôtel de Ville, Monsieur Bailly, the mayor of Paris, placed the popular cockade in the king’s hat and addressed him. The king was unprepared and unable to answer, Jefferson wrote, so Bailly gathered scraps of his sentences and made out an answer to deliver to the audience as though it came from the king. On the return journey, the cries became “vive le roy et la nation”. A bourgeois guard conducted the king to Versailles.

The Bastille episode moved through signs, offices, armed bodies, and public speech. A flag of truce restrained the crowd long enough for a deputation to approach. A discharge broke that interval. The crowd’s attack ended the fortress’s control, but people inside it released prisoners and surviving defenders. The governor’s death was made into a public triumph, while the king’s return was surrounded by a guard and addressed through a cockade. Authority was challenged, seized, killed, displayed, negotiated with, and partially reassembled within one day.

Jefferson’s narrative is revealing because it does not present the crowd as a single undifferentiated body. The deputies could persuade people to fall back. The crowd could rush forward after the deputies withdrew. Some garrison members were killed, others released. The king was met by citizens carrying weapons and by officials who still spoke in the language of public office. Each action depended on a different relation between people and authority. The assault required collective movement against the fortress; the release required a decision that prisoners and surviving defenders should be freed; the procession required bodies, weapons, officials, and symbols to occupy the city in a recognizable order.

Jefferson knew that the Bastille had been taken, that arms and prisoners had changed hands, and that the governor and lieutenant governor had been killed. The crowd’s entry remained unknown to him. The statements of alleged participants were too contradictory for him to accept. The means of entry would tell us how much planning, improvisation, military skill, or fortunate opportunity shaped the seizure. The record preserves the result more securely than the procedure.

A crowd can be politically effective without having a single plan, and a politically meaningful event can contain actions that were neither planned by one authority nor random in every detail. On 14 July, the deputation, the flags, the gunfire, the assault, the release of prisoners, the execution of officials, and the royal procession were connected by an unfolding crisis. Their connection arose through proximity, communication, visible symbols, and a weakening claim to obedience, without requiring one shared motive.

Jefferson’s choice of sequence assigns political weight to the transitions. His account begins with a request for arms, not with an abstract declaration about revolution. The Bastille appears first as a defended place containing weapons and governed by a named official. When the discharge kills four people near the deputies, the request becomes an armed confrontation. After the deputies retire, the people’s rush becomes intelligible as a response within the narrative, though the record does not state what each participant thought the gunfire meant.

The phrase “a great collection of people” is also important. Jefferson does not provide the crowd’s exact number at the fortress, and he does not divide it into occupational, political, or neighbourhood groups. He gives no roll of participants. The crowd appears instead as a public presence capable of falling back, rushing forward, taking arms, releasing captives, and carrying officials’ severed heads through Paris. Its collective force is visible in action, while its internal composition remains indistinct.

That indistinctness changes when Jefferson describes the later procession. There he gives a number: about 60,000 citizens. He names the States General, La Fayette, bourgeois guards, Bailly, the Hôtel de Ville, Versailles, and the Palais Royal. The crowd is no longer only the force gathered before a fortress. It occupies the streets around a king and a national political body. The Bastille’s arms become part of the procession’s visible equipment, linking the earlier seizure to the later demonstration. The same day contains a crowd at the edge of a military prison and a crowd surrounding the monarch.

Jefferson’s account of the king’s speech introduces another form of collective power. Bailly places the popular cockade in the king’s hat, then supplies an answer when the king cannot respond adequately. The mayor does not simply report a royal statement; he constructs a public reply from “some scraps of sentences” and delivers it to the audience as from the king. The scene makes legitimacy depend on reception. The king’s presence alone does not settle what he means. His words must be gathered, shaped, and presented by another official before the audience can receive them.

The procession’s cries register that alteration. “Vive la nation” dominates the first passage, while “vive le roy et la nation” appears on the return. Jefferson calls the king’s passage an “Amende honorable”, a public act of submission or acknowledgment, and describes it as one “no sovereign ever made, and no people ever received”. The language is ceremonial, but it follows a day in which royal force at the Bastille has been defeated and royal authority has been carried through streets lined with armed citizens. Ceremony gives the new balance of power a public form.

The seven prisoners in the National Archives exhibit sharpen Jefferson’s emphasis on the Bastille as symbol. If the fortress contained two mentally ill people, four forgers, and one person incarcerated for incest, the event cannot be explained by the immediate rescue of a large captive population. The crowd’s act acquired meaning from the institution’s association with royal power, from the arms inside it, and from the crisis surrounding the monarchy. The prison’s actual population and its political image belonged to different registers, and both were active in the event.

The difference also affects the meaning of release. Jefferson’s sentence joins the prisoners and surviving members of the garrison as those whom the crowd discharged. Release extended to people who could represent revolutionary innocence as well as defenders who had not been killed in the first fury. The sentence does not tell us who made the decision, whether it was contested, or how the prisoners and soldiers were treated afterwards. It does show that the assault did not produce indiscriminate killing of everyone inside the fortress. Even amid lethal retaliation, selection and restraint remained possible.

The phrase “first moment of fury” gives Jefferson’s interpretation a temporal boundary. He treats the opening violence as intense but brief, after which some people were spared. That wording may be his own characterization rather than a neutral measurement, yet it guides his account towards a distinction between the crowd’s initial violence and the later acts of release. The governor and lieutenant governor were singled out for execution while others survived. The governor was not merely killed. He was taken to the Grève, identified as a place of public execution, beheaded, and represented through the carrying of his head to the Palais Royal. The lieutenant governor underwent the same fate in Jefferson’s sentence. The route transformed official deaths into a statement addressed to Paris.

Even without a formal government, a political crowd can produce symbols. It can seize an existing site, take its weapons, free its prisoners, and carry the remains of its officials through the city. Yet the procession around the king shows that revolutionary action also depended on offices and forms inherited from the order being challenged. The States General walked beside the carriage. La Fayette appeared as commander in chief. Bailly addressed the king as mayor. Bourgeois guards escorted him to Versailles. The day’s new authority was assembled from crowd action, representative bodies, municipal office, militia, and royal presence.

The absence of a reliable account of entry leaves room for the interpretation that the seizure was chiefly spontaneous crowd violence. The decisive fact, on that reading, is the sudden rush after four people were killed. The crowd did not proceed according to a recorded plan, and the participants who later claimed knowledge gave conflicting accounts. Jefferson’s remark that their stories destroyed one another’s credibility supports caution about assigning a coherent strategy to the assault. The dead, the rush, the seizure of arms, and the executions can appear as the escalation of a public confrontation that exceeded the intentions of the deputation.

That explanation has force. The record does not provide a committee order, a written assault plan, a list of commanders, or a reliable account of the passage through the fortress. It does not identify the exact number of people before the Bastille. Nor does it disclose the private motives of Corny, the five other deputies, de Launay, the garrison, or those who rushed forward. Any account that turns the entire crowd into a disciplined organisation claims more than Jefferson’s passage supports.

Spontaneity does not describe the whole episode. Before the rush, a deputation approached with a demand for arms. A flag of truce was planted and answered. The people were persuaded to fall back. Someone had selected representatives, and those representatives acted in a setting where the crowd could respond to their intervention. The crowd’s movement was not simply a private quarrel multiplied by numbers. It was directed, however temporarily, by signs and persons whose authority mattered enough to alter the position of the people outside the fortress.

Nor did the crowd’s actions end with the seizure. The people took the arms, released the prisoners and surviving garrison members, carried the governor and lieutenant governor to the Grève, and carried their heads to the Palais Royal. These acts may not have followed one master plan, but they involved choices about what to seize, whom to release, whom to kill, and how to display the dead. A completely spontaneous account would need to explain why the crowd’s violence had these particular targets and why the episode continued as a public procession.

The organised-action interpretation requires equal restraint. It is tempting to treat the deputation as evidence that the assault was planned from the beginning, with the flag of truce serving as a tactical device and the crowd waiting for an appointed moment. Jefferson’s text does not establish that. The deputies’ demand was for arms, not explicitly for the fortress’s capture. The exchange of flags could indicate negotiation, confusion, or an attempt to control the crowd without a settled plan for what would follow. The fortress was taken, but the route of entry is unknown.

Organisation can be located at several scales without being projected onto every participant. The deputation was a small organised act. The crowd’s ability to fall back was a moment of collective responsiveness. The assault was coordinated in the minimal sense that many people acted towards the same place. The seizure of arms and release of prisoners produced consequences that were publicly intelligible. None of this proves that the crowd possessed a unified command or a common motive.

The Swedish allotment system, described through Charles XI’s reorganisation and the Military Act passed on 27 October 1682, offers a useful contrast in the kind of coordination it made visible. Contracts with counties and provinces specified obligations, and a rote of two to four farmers maintained an infantry soldier with equipment, a croft, and farmland. The arrangement could bring soldiers to a company meeting place in a couple of days and to a regimental meeting place in around a week. The Bastille crowd had no comparable documentary chain of obligation in the evidence here. Its power arose in a crisis at the point of action, not from a recorded system that assigned each participant a place in advance.

The comparison clarifies the difference between administrative mobilisation and collective political action. A standing army can be assembled through contracts and prepared routes. A crowd can become effective through deputies, signals, shared attention, and recognition of a symbolic target. One form of coordination is routinised; the other may be compressed into hours. The Swedish system made military capacity durable and repeatable. The Bastille shows how quickly collective action could become politically meaningful when ordinary authority lost legitimacy.

The fortress’s symbolic status helps explain why an event involving seven prisoners could have consequences beyond the prison population. The National Archives exhibit describes the Bastille as a place imagined to contain vast numbers of people who had displeased the king, even though its actual prisoners on 14 July were two mentally ill people, four forgers, and one person imprisoned for incest. The gap between the imagined prison and the occupied building did not prevent action. It supplied a language through which the seizure could be understood as an attack on arbitrary royal power.

Symbols did not act alone. The crowd had to confront a governor and garrison, endure a discharge that Jefferson says killed four people, acquire weapons, and decide what to do with those who remained inside. Symbolic legitimacy shaped the target, while physical force determined possession. The Bastille’s meaning could magnify the event, but it could not open the gates or carry the arms into Paris. Collective action joined interpretation to bodily risk.

The subsequent procession complicates the idea that the crowd’s politics consisted only of hostility towards monarchy. Jefferson records “vive la nation” in the streets, then “vive le roy et la nation” on the return. The king remained on the scene, displayed within an arrangement in which the States General, La Fayette, bourgeois guards, Bailly, and armed citizens surrounded him. The crowd challenged royal authority while participating in a public performance that still included the king. Political legitimacy was being renegotiated, not simply erased.

The killings at the Grève do not prove that restraint had disappeared. The governor and lieutenant governor were executed, but surviving garrison members were released. Prisoners were discharged. A flag of truce was honoured long enough for the deputation to advance, and the people fell back when persuaded. Jefferson’s account shows negotiation and selection alongside lethal retaliation, though it does not establish that the people involved at each moment were the same. The violence was uneven, directed through judgements that the record only partly reveals.

The account does not tell us whether the crowd understood itself as defending Paris, demanding weapons, liberating prisoners, overthrowing royal tyranny, or responding to the deaths near the deputies. Those possibilities may have overlapped, and different participants may have held different ones. The evidence supports a claim about public action more securely than a claim about interior conviction. People gathered, responded to a deputation, rushed the fortress, seized its arms, released some captives, killed two officials, and carried their heads through the city. Their motives remain more difficult to assign.

What, then, can the Bastille record establish about those motives? Jefferson’s narrative can establish that a deputation led by Monsieur de Corny and five others went to ask Monsieur de Launay for arms on the afternoon of 14 July 1789. It can establish that a flag of truce was planted and answered, that the people fell back somewhat, and that four people nearest the deputies were killed by a discharge from the Bastille. It can establish the order Jefferson gives after that moment: the deputies retired, the people rushed, and the fortification was taken.

Those facts permit careful inferences about circumstances. The crowd was already present before the deputation arrived. Arms were important enough to be the stated object of the mission. The Bastille was defended by a garrison Jefferson described as 100 men and as a fortress of great strength. Its seizure was followed by the taking of weapons and the release of the prisoners and surviving garrison members. The National Archives exhibit identifies the prisoners as seven people: two who were mentally ill, four forgers, and one person incarcerated for incest. The governor and lieutenant governor were then carried to the Grève, killed, and represented through a procession to the Palais Royal.

The same facts do not tell us whether the people before the Bastille shared one purpose. The record gives no names for the four killed nearest the deputies. It gives no number for the crowd at the fortress. It gives no full dialogue between the deputation and de Launay. Jefferson says that those claiming to have taken part offered conflicting stories about how the crowd entered, and he treats those stories as mutually discrediting. The event’s outcome is therefore more certain than its participants’ explanations of what they did.

The seven prisoners sharpen the question of motive rather than answer it. The crowd’s action cannot be assigned simply to the immediate need to rescue a mass of political prisoners. The prison’s imagined population and its actual occupants diverged. A participant might have acted for arms, against the garrison, for the release of captives, against royal authority, or because the fortress had become the available object through which a larger crisis could be confronted. The record does not sort these motives.

Nor does the later procession settle the matter. About 60,000 citizens, in Jefferson’s estimate, lined the route with muskets, pistols, swords, pikes, pruning hooks, and scythes. They cried “vive la nation” while the king’s carriage moved between the States General and bourgeois guards. Bailly placed the popular cockade in the king’s hat and fashioned a public answer from scraps of the king’s sentences. On the return, the cry became “vive le roy et la nation”, and a bourgeois guard conducted the king to Versailles. These actions show a public negotiation over legitimacy, but they do not reveal whether each person accepted the same political settlement or merely joined a powerful procession.

A motive can be inferred from a choice only within limits. Carrying the governor’s head to the Palais Royal made the killing communicative, yet the record does not state what each carrier intended to communicate. Taking the Bastille’s arms made the crowd more capable of force, yet the passage does not show who planned to use them or against whom. Releasing surviving garrison members indicates restraint in the aftermath, but it does not disclose whether mercy, calculation, command, or exhaustion shaped the decision.

The unanswered question is not whether the crowd acted politically. Its actions altered control of a royal fortress, transferred weapons, freed prisoners, killed officials, and helped produce a procession in which the king appeared under changed conditions. The sharper question is how many political meanings were carried by the same actions, and how they were distributed among the people who performed them.

Jefferson’s uncertainty about entry preserves that problem. The Bastille was taken, but the record cannot identify the reliable path by which the crowd entered. The prisoners were released, while the record leaves unknown who ordered or negotiated their release. The governor and lieutenant governor were killed and displayed, with the deliberation behind those acts undisclosed. The king was escorted to Versailles, but the cries of the procession shifted between nation and king-and-nation without revealing what every participant believed.

Crowd violence is often made easier to narrate by assigning it one intention. The Bastille record resists that convenience. It offers named people, a date, a place, flags, weapons, deaths, prisoners, offices, and routes through Paris. These particulars show collective action moving through institutional breakdown and symbolic authority. They also leave motives plural, uneven, and partly inaccessible. The event can be understood as revolutionary without turning every participant into a conscious architect of revolution, and as violent without treating violence as the only act the crowd performed.

On 20 May 1903, Herbert Samuel rose in the British House of Commons and moved a resolution about the Congo Free State. The wording carried the promise made when the state was established: its African subjects were to be governed with humanity, and no trading monopoly or privilege was to be permitted within its territory. The resolution asked the British government to confer with the other signatories of the Berlin General Act so that measures might be adopted “to abate the evils prevalent in that State.” A legal framework, a commercial prohibition, a population described as subjects, and an appeal between European powers were joined in one sentence. The distance between the language of colonial rule and the conduct performed in its name had become a parliamentary question.

Balfour’s government then instructed Roger Casement, the British consul at Boma, to investigate conditions in the Congo Free State. Casement was Irish. His report was published in 1904. It comprised forty pages of Parliamentary Papers, with another twenty pages of individual statements appended to it. The statements had been gathered by Casement as consul.

The appended statements named the forms of harm with a bluntness that official language usually avoided. They included allegations of “killings, mutilations, kidnappings and cruel beatings” of the native population by soldiers of King Leopold’s Congo Administration, as the summary of the report records. Each term indicated a different act. Killing removed life; mutilation altered the body; kidnapping seized a person; beating inflicted pain through a direct exercise of force. The report kept them distinct, placing them beside one another as allegations attached to soldiers of the Congo Administration.

A mutilated body is evidence of injury. A kidnapped person is evidence of seizure and removal. The report also records a shooting during a rubber-collection expedition in 1903. Its words do not establish the same relationship between victim and perpetrator in every case, and they do not allow every incident to be reconstructed in full. They show that the violence was being described not as a quarrel between unrelated individuals but as conduct associated with soldiers of the Congo Administration.

The report’s physical proportions also mattered. Forty pages of Parliamentary Papers and twenty pages of individual statements gave a government document a double form. Its first part entered the language of official review; its appendix carried accounts gathered by a consul. When copies went to the Belgian government and to the other signatories of the 1885 Berlin Agreement, the allegations moved through the same international channels that had helped authorize the territory’s political existence. A complaint about local acts became a question addressed to states.

The British Parliament demanded a meeting of the fourteen signatory powers to review the Berlin Agreement. Yet the report’s route did not guarantee immediate transformation. It was issued as a Command paper in 1904 and laid before the Houses of Parliament, while the original was not published in full until 1985 in an annotated book by two Belgian historians of colonialism. Reports may circulate officially while the testimony within them remains difficult for a wider public to read. Administrative visibility and public accessibility are not the same thing.

In Belgium, the report entered a different political struggle. Emile Vandervelde and other critics of Leopold’s Congo policy pressed Parliament to force the king to establish an independent commission of enquiry. The summary of the commission states that its findings confirmed Casement’s report in every detail. During the process, people responsible for murders during a 1903 rubber-collection expedition were arrested and punished. One Belgian national received a five-year sentence for causing the shooting of at least 122 Congolese natives.

The number in that sentence connects a large injury to a judicial consequence, but it does not measure all the deaths or all the violence associated with Congo rule. Nor does the existence of a commission erase the killings that led to its creation. Investigation followed harm; it did not prevent the harm already recorded.

Leopold retained personal control of the Congo until 1908, when the Parliament of Belgium annexed the Congo Free State and assumed its administration as the Belgian Congo. The change converted one governing form into another, while the report, the commission, the arrests, and the sentence demonstrated that the old system had become politically difficult to defend. Reform here was neither the opposite of coercion nor proof that coercion had ended. It was a response produced by investigation, publicity, parliamentary pressure, and punishment.

The Casement Report sits between several kinds of action. Roger Casement investigated. Herbert Samuel moved a resolution. Balfour’s government instructed a consul. Congolese witnesses supplied statements. Soldiers were accused of killing, mutilating, kidnapping, and beating. Belgian politicians pressed Leopold. A commission examined the allegations. One Belgian national received a five-year sentence. Parliament annexed the territory. The document makes the sequence of extraction and scrutiny visible, even where it leaves the individual circumstances of the testimony beyond recovery. Colonial violence entered an administrative record, and the record became one instrument through which colonial rule was challenged.

The question is how such violence became ordinary enough to be administered. A concessionary system required more than a desire for rubber. It required a territory claimed by a government, companies or officials assigned access to production, soldiers available to enforce demands, and records capable of converting labour into expected quantities. The Congo evidence identifies the soldiers of the Congo Administration, but the reviewed passages do not provide the precise company accounts, local orders, collection quotas, or daily procedures by which every demand was made. The broad structure is visible; its local machinery is unevenly preserved.

A production system can make aggression routine without requiring every administrator to repeat the same act. The state defines who may demand labour. A concession assigns an economic interest to a place or resource. A tax or production obligation turns time spent gathering rubber into a duty owed to the governing power. Soldiers make refusal dangerous. Officials receive reports about what has been collected. When the amount is judged insufficient, force can be applied and then recorded as discipline, punishment, or an incident in the maintenance of order. The sequence does not make violence automatic, but it places violence inside a repeatable path.

The Congo Free State’s international language sharpened this contradiction. The Berlin framework promised humane government and rejected trading monopolies or privileges, while the system associated with Leopold’s personal rule produced allegations against soldiers during rubber collection. The legal promise did not restrain extraction by itself. A rule that exists only as a declaration can be overtaken by the office that controls soldiers, territory, and access to production. The force of a document depends on who can inspect conduct, who can punish violations, and whether those subject to the rule can make their experiences heard.

Earlier, the Zong case showed how a commercial claim could translate the killing of enslaved people into the language of insured property. The Congo case extends that institutional problem from a ship’s accounting to territorial government. Here the relevant question was not only how a death might be valued after it occurred. It was how an administration could make people, land, labour, and output legible to offices that demanded results. A person forced into production could be counted as a worker, a taxpayer, a subject, or an obstacle. Each category made a different response seem available to those who held power.

The geography between the people who demanded production, those who enforced it, and the office that might later investigate could conceal violence, delay accountability, and allow officials to describe coercion as necessary administration.

Yet distance could be crossed. Casement’s position at Boma gave him an official route into the territory and a form of authority with which to gather statements. The British House of Commons supplied a forum. The Belgian Parliament supplied another. The fourteen signatories of the Berlin Agreement became a possible audience because the Congo Free State had been linked to an international act. Administrative connection enlarged the field in which violence could occur, but it also created channels through which evidence could travel. The same kinds of papers that defined rights and territory could authorize extraction or expose it. A commission could be established because a monarch’s policy was under pressure; its findings could lead to arrests without undoing the system that had made the investigation necessary. The annexation of 1908 changed the sovereign form of Congo rule, but the available passages do not provide a full account of the labour practices or violence that followed under Belgian administration. A change in office should not be mistaken for a completed change in the relation between production and coercion.

What made refusal visible to the administration? Was it a missing quantity, an absent worker, a delayed delivery, a village that did not comply, or an official’s report that described disorder? The question cannot be settled from the summarized allegations alone, but it directs attention toward the smallest links in the chain. Forced production becomes routine when a demand can be issued repeatedly, when noncompliance can be recognized, when soldiers can be sent, and when the resulting harm can be absorbed into an account of order.

The Maji Maji uprising in German East Africa reveals that chain from another direction. There, the record begins not with a parliamentary inquiry but with a production demand that helped turn colonial administration into armed rebellion. German policy was designed to force the indigenous population to grow cotton for export. The crop belonged to a colonial economy, but the labour and land required to produce it belonged to African communities whose own subsistence was disrupted by the demand. The conflict that followed was therefore not simply a dispute over a commodity. It was a struggle over who could direct agricultural work and what consequences followed refusal.

The war began in 1905 in German East Africa, in the territory that is now Tanzania. The rebellion was an armed uprising of Africans against German colonial rule. The record separately identifies leaders and traditional healers among those involved. It does not establish how every participant understood the movement or how its internal connections were formed.

Cotton gave the conflict a material centre. German officials wanted export production; African people were compelled to cultivate it. The available account does not specify the local orders, places, or exact methods used to enforce cultivation, so the policy cannot be reconstructed field by field. Its consequence is clearer. A colonial government attempted to redirect agricultural labour toward a crop chosen for export, and the policy helped produce an armed response.

The shift from cultivation to rebellion did not occur because cotton itself was violent. The violence arose from the authority attached to the crop. A government that could compel planting could also decide which work counted, how much land should be used, and what penalty accompanied refusal. The demand entered the household and the field before it entered the battlefield. German rule made agriculture an administrative matter, then encountered resistance when the people expected to perform that labour treated the demand as an attack on their ability to govern their own lives.

Maji Maji was not a single army formed under one command in the manner of a European regiment. The account describes an armed rebellion of Africans against German rule and separately identifies leaders and traditional healers. Its internal organisation remains only partly known. The word “rebels,” however, describes their relation to Germany, not the whole range of interests within the communities involved.

German authority responded to the uprising as a military and administrative problem. The war lasted from 1905 to 1907. During that period, the colonial government confronted armed fighters. The policy later described as scorched earth attacked the conditions that allowed resistance to continue. Gustav Adolf von Götzen, the governor of German East Africa, was associated with the policy, which the available account connects to the famine that followed the war.

A letter written in 1905 by Captain Wangenheim makes the intended relation between hunger and submission unusually explicit. He wrote to von Götzen, “Only hunger and want can bring about a final submission. Military actions alone will remain more or less a drop in the ocean.” The sentence distinguishes military action from the deprivation that would make military resistance unsustainable. Hunger is not described as an accidental by-product. It is presented as the means by which submission might finally be secured.

That letter gives a sequence to the policy. German forces confronted resistance. Wangenheim judged military operations insufficient. Hunger and want were proposed as the stronger instrument. Scorched earth then connected military suppression to the destruction of food security. The record does not list every village burned, field destroyed, or store emptied, and it does not establish the detailed chronology of each action. It does establish the reasoning expressed by one German military leader and the wider association between scorched-earth policy and famine.

The human cost was enormous, though the estimate is wide. Between 75,000 and 300,000 people died during the war, overwhelmingly from famine, according to the cited account. The range itself signals the difficulty of counting deaths across a territory where conflict, hunger, and displacement were connected. A famine death is not the same event as a battlefield killing, even when military policy contributed to the conditions of famine. To destroy or seize the means of subsistence can turn food into a weapon and make death spread beyond the immediate reach of soldiers.

This was the colonial administration’s power in its most expansive form. A cotton policy directed labour. A military response targeted rebellion. A scorched-earth policy affected food. A governor’s decision and a captain’s letter connected the field of production to the survival of a population. The system made access to land, crops, and stored food vulnerable to armed authority, allowing hunger to serve political ends without directly killing every person.

Resistance remained active within that pressure. Von Götzen was willing to pardon common soldiers who gave up their weapons. The available passage also refers to leaders and traditional healers, but it does not establish that they were offered the same treatment. The passage does not identify those people or explain how the pardon operated in particular places. It shows that punishment and mercy were both instruments of administration, applied according to a classification made by the governor.

A pardon can seem to contradict a policy of destruction, but the contradiction is only apparent. Punishment removes or incapacitates opponents; pardon can separate ordinary fighters from leaders, encourage disarmament, and weaken a movement’s capacity to continue. The same government could destroy food supplies while offering conditional mercy to those who surrendered. Coercion did not require one unchanging level of violence. It required the power to decide when a person was an enemy, when an enemy might be spared, and what surrender involved.

The administrative language of German rule met resistance in the bodies of people expected to choose between submission, resistance, and flight. German authority sought to make bullets less important by producing hunger. The rebels faced a colonial government that possessed firearms, offices, and the ability to attack food production across a wide area.

The result was an unequal contest in which Africans acted as more than victims waiting for European decisions. The uprising required people to act, to join a movement, to accept risk, and to direct violence against colonial rule. Its internal relationships remain partly unknown. The rebellion altered the colonial calculation. German officials had to decide not only how to fight armed opponents but how far to punish the population among whom resistance lived.

German policy then widened the meaning of the target. If a rebel could not be easily separated from a community that grew food, carried supplies, or refused cotton, the community itself could be treated as part of the military problem. Scorched earth erased the boundary between combat and subsistence. Farms, food, and people became connected in the colonial response. Famine belongs in the history of the uprising without being reduced to a casualty figure because it records the extension of war into the means by which civilians survived.

The aftermath carried the violence forward. The war ended in 1907, and the Great Hunger followed it. The cited account attributes the famine in large part to the scorched-earth policies used by von Götzen to suppress the rebellion.

The estimate of 75,000 to 300,000 deaths gives the famine a scale but not a complete social map. It does not identify which communities lost the greatest share of their people, how food was distributed, or how survivors moved through the crisis. It does show that the principal form of death was famine rather than direct battlefield killing. Here the category of atrocity must include policy that made hunger deliberate or foreseeable, while keeping hunger distinct from a shooting, a beating, or a battlefield death.

Wangenheim’s sentence is central because it names the purpose as “final submission.” Hunger was not merely a condition in which rebellion happened to weaken. It was presented as a method of ending resistance. Military action alone was a “drop in the ocean,” while deprivation promised a submission that force in the field could not secure. Colonial authority thus treated the population’s capacity to eat as part of the military theatre.

At the same time, von Götzen’s willingness to pardon common soldiers who surrendered their weapons reveals a second calculation. A colonial government that sought total submission still needed distinctions among opponents. Common fighters, leaders, and traditional healers were not necessarily placed in the same category. Surrender could be made attractive to one group while famine was imposed upon the wider population. The policy combined selective mercy with collective pressure. That combination helps explain how colonial rule could survive a rebellion while leaving behind deep destruction.

The record does not name the leaders who received or were denied pardon, and it does not specify the local communities through which surrender occurred. Those absences should prevent a general account of African collaboration or resistance from being built out of this one episode. What can be seen is narrower and solid: German authority connected agricultural coercion to rebellion, military force to food destruction, and surrender to conditional mercy. The colonial government used more than one instrument because it governed more than one kind of relation.

Beyond the preserved statements, African communities had to navigate choices that colonial documents tend to flatten. A person could support resistance, provide food under pressure, cooperate with officials, conceal information, flee, surrender, or change position as military conditions altered. These actions need not express a single political belief. Survival could require compliance in one moment and refusal in another. A village official or soldier might serve the colonial state while remaining connected to people harmed by it. The available Congo and Maji Maji records do not allow these variations to be mapped in detail, and they do not document each one.

The record identifies soldiers of King Leopold’s Congo Administration in the allegations recorded by Casement. It does not identify those soldiers as the Force Publique or establish the composition of that force from the passages used here.

The same caution applies to the Maji Maji movement. The record does not show that every group joined, or that every participant agreed on the purposes of resistance. Some communities may have acted together against cotton cultivation; others may have faced the uprising, the German army, or famine from different positions. The sources preserved here leave those differences unidentified. They show Africans responding to European action within the colonial relationship.

A mechanism of survival could therefore begin with classification. German officials distinguished common soldiers from other categories of opponents. Congo authorities distinguished soldiers, producers, subjects, and alleged offenders. Such categories made different forms of treatment possible. A person classified as a surrendering soldier might receive pardon; one classified as a leader might remain a target; a community classified as supporting rebels might face the destruction of food. The category did not merely describe a person. It helped determine what the government could do to that person.

Next came the circulation of information. Colonial soldiers and officials reported resistance, production, and disorder upward. African people carried knowledge of military movements, food supplies, punishments, and opportunities for escape across local networks. The documents preserve more of the first kind of reporting than the second. Casement’s appended statements partially reverse that imbalance by carrying African allegations into official proceedings. The Maji Maji record, by contrast, preserves Wangenheim’s letter more clearly than the voices of the people enduring the famine.

Then came the choice imposed by unequal force. A community might be compelled to cultivate cotton, pressured to supply food, or threatened by soldiers. Resistance could turn a production dispute into armed conflict; collaboration could reduce immediate punishment while strengthening the colonial system; withdrawal could protect some people while abandoning others to official suspicion. These alternatives were constrained, not freely chosen. The existence of a choice under coercion does not make the relationship equal.

Finally, consequences fed back into the system. A report could prompt investigation, as the Casement Report did. Investigation could produce arrests and a sentence. Parliamentary pressure could produce annexation in 1908. In German East Africa, military resistance led to scorched earth, famine, and conditional pardon. Administrative power moved in multiple directions: it extracted, classified, and punished, while also generating evidence, controversy, reform, and new forms of political action.

The Congo and Maji Maji cases leave different records because they are different historical situations. Casement’s forty pages and twenty pages of statements show allegations carried through consular and parliamentary channels. Wangenheim’s 1905 letter shows a military calculation about hunger and submission. One record helped expose a concessionary regime; the other helps reveal how a colonial government attempted to break a rebellion. Neither supplies the full interior life of the people caught within the system. Still, both cases connect production to authority. Rubber collection and forced cotton cultivation were not simply economic activities performed under difficult conditions. They were demands backed by governments, soldiers, and punishments. The resulting violence included direct injury, kidnapping, and shooting, but also the destruction of food and the pressure of famine. Resistance took the form of testimony in one case and armed uprising in the other. Reform appeared through commissions, punishment, and annexation, while survival required choices that remain only partly recorded.

Colonial violence was a relationship that moved through offices, fields, expeditions, courts, parliaments, letters, and armed movements. Although colonial systems often tried to classify their victims as passive objects, those subjected to them acted within and against those classifications. Administrators varied, yet they acted within structures that could make coercion routine. The Casement Report carried the allegations to governments, while the Maji Maji record associates forced production with rebellion and famine. Between them lies a history of extraction investigated, resisted, punished, and only partially reformed.

chapters.title: Industrial War and the Civilian Population
chapters.markdown:
While working as the United States consul at Harput, Leslie Davis watched large groups of Armenians pass along a route from provinces beyond Harput toward the Der Zor desert in Syria. His record gives no date for the passage, no number of deportees, and no names of the officials who directed them. It gives a place, a witness, and a movement: Armenians were deported from provinces outside Harput toward the desert. Davis reported that some groups were rerouted in Harput, “only to be butchered in this province.”

“Rerouted” carries a cold administrative weight. It describes a change in direction, perhaps made by men whose names Davis did not record, but it does not disclose the chain by which that change became possible. It places the deportees within a process without showing the order, office, timetable, or means of transmission. A convoy could be redirected by a local official, an escort, a military command, or an instruction arriving from elsewhere. The account does not settle which. It records the consequence of movement being controlled: deportees were exposed to a new destination, and Davis associated that altered route with killing in Harput province.

His observations of groups arriving from farther north sharpen the scene. The convoys contained no men, he noted. The surviving members were “much abused, starved and exhausted.” These are not interchangeable signs of suffering. Abuse indicates treatment by other people, though the passage does not identify the perpetrators or the acts. Starvation describes a condition of hunger without establishing whether it resulted from deliberate policy, seizure of supplies, neglect, or the conditions of movement. Exhaustion records a bodily state produced by prolonged strain. Each word marks a different relation between the deportees and the process carrying them onward.

The absence of men is equally difficult to compress into one explanation. Davis did not say where they had gone, when they had disappeared, or how many had once belonged to the convoys. His statement records a visible fact at Harput: the groups arriving from the north had no men among them. Their condition made the convoy evidence of earlier violence, even though the account does not explain that violence in detail.

Harput was a place where routes changed and the character of deportation became visible. People arrived from the north without men; people were directed toward Der Zor; some groups were sent along a different route and, Davis reported, killed in the province. The account links rerouting to slaughter and records abuse, starvation, and exhaustion among those who survived.

That account differs from a battlefield report. Davis was not describing opposing armies meeting, a contested position changing hands, or a supply line cut by an enemy. He was describing people being moved over distance, with the movement accompanied by reported killing and severe suffering. The account shows deportation as more than a change of residence.
